source.title: Beyond Token Scale: Chunk-Level Sparse Autoencoders for Reliable Semantic Feature Discovery
source.authors: Xu Wang; Yi-Fan Yang; Ting-Ting Yu; Di-Fan Zou

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether SAE features in a real language model capture semantic content, extending the feature-discovery question to Qwen3.5-9B-Base rather than reproducing the toy-model superposition method.
record.gate_note: The paper directly evaluates SAE feature explanations, semantic-feature prevalence, feature persistence, dictionary utilization, cue-free reasoning detection, and feature steering. Retrieval, classification, and document-neighborhood results are downstream uses of frozen SAE codes; they do not directly measure superposition or whether the codes recover semantic features, so they are not rows. Numbers used only to select settings are also excluded.
record.test_reason: This is a methods paper. It trains token-level and chunk-level SAEs on Qwen3.5-9B-Base and compares their feature quality: semantic fraction, InterpScore, persistence, utilization, reasoning detection and steering. SAE decomposition is used as a tool. No result asks whether the model's activations are superposed or spread across neurons. No interpretability baseline is given (neurons, random directions, untrained model), so the existence of 'recoverable sparse features' is assumed rather than tested. The rows compare the authors' methods against other SAE variants, not measurements of the claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that chunk-level SAEs keep target-relative fidelity while yielding more reliable semantic features than token-level SAEs. They describe Mean-Chunk as best for high-level feature discovery, cue-free reasoning detection and steering, and Cross-Chunk as best for retrieval, classification transfer, persistence and utilization.
record.recipe_differences: This study trains and evaluates token- and chunk-level SAEs on a language model; it does not reproduce the original toy-network superposition setup or its feature-geometry experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: SAE architecture and prediction objective affect semantic-feature fractions and explanation scores; the paper also reports that Joint-Chunk partner weight changes the balance of capabilities.

fits_no_version.finding: With the same model, layer, data, width and sparsity, changing the SAE's input unit and target roughly doubles the semantic-feature fraction (17.2% to 34.8%). It also changes which features are found (Figure 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The features an SAE recovers depend substantially on its training objective and input granularity. This bears on whether dictionary features are canonical (V5), but the study does not frame or test it that way.

record.problems: Evidence is from one model checkpoint. Semantic interpretation and steering rely on LLM judges; reasoning examples and paired controls are generated and rewritten. The authors note that the ArXiv evaluation does not establish absence of source-corpus pre-exposure because the Pile contains ArXiv material.
record.rows_left_out: Retrieval, classification, and document-neighborhood results are reported in Sections 5.1, 5.3, and Appendix E, but are downstream evaluations of frozen codes rather than direct measurements of the claim's superposition geometry or semantic-feature recovery.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity sweep, or geometry analysis.
No test of capacity or importance as the cause of polysemanticity.
No neuron-level distribution analysis. SAE feature recovery is not compared against any non-SAE baseline; only SAE variants are compared.
Completeness, stability across seeds, and canonicality are not tested. The dictionaries' dependence on objective is noted only descriptively.
No comparison of one-dimensional and multi-dimensional features.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 'supports' label rests on method-comparison rows with no baseline relevant to the claim, so all labels are removed. The study is a T4 tool use of SAEs. Steering values in Figure 7B are readable and should replace 'figure only'. Judge and generator are LLMs (DeepSeek V4).

versions.untested_parts: No small toy networks, feature-versus-dimension sweep, sparsity-dependent transition, or superposition geometry is tested.
The paper does not test whether feature importance determines dedicated dimensions versus sharing, or whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity.
No alternative cause of polysemantic neurons is tested.
It evaluates semantic and functional properties of SAE features in one model, but does not measure how many neurons each feature spans or whether activations are distributed across neurons.
Feature interpretability and persistence across passages are measured, but completeness, canonicality, and stability of SAE features as the model's units are not tested.
No comparison of one-dimensional directions with multidimensional features is made.

rows.subject: Qwen3.5-9B-Base

rows.baseline: BatchTopK utilization is more than five times lower
rows.note: The paper reports utilization over five times BatchTopK's level.
rows.check: Utilization of the dictionary's own codes is a property of the SAE, not of the model's representation.

rows.subject: Qwen3.5-9B-Base
rows.operation_detail: Tested whether a frozen feature selected for backtracking detects the relation in held-out passages after removing familiar verbal cues.
rows.uncertainty: Matched reasoning audit uses 20,000 paired bootstrap resamples; interval values not stated here
rows.note: The paper says this tests recognition of the relation after removing words such as “wait.”
rows.check: Downstream reasoning-detection performance of the study's own method.

rows.subject: Qwen3.5-9B-Base
rows.operation_detail: Tested whether selected token-level SAE features detect backtracking in held-out passages after familiar verbal cues are removed.
rows.uncertainty: Matched reasoning audit uses 20,000 paired bootstrap resamples; interval values not stated here
rows.note: The paper reports the two token baselines together and does not give separate values in the text.
rows.check: The state 'partial' is wrong: under 5% recall is near-absent detection. In any case it is a comparator method's downstream performance, not a measure of the claim.
